lesson.text: Quick memory: what did the Maya use for zero? (A shell.) This year you met Greece, Persia, Rome, India, Han China and the Maya. Today: what they gave us, and how to compare them like a historian.
From Greece: democracy, theatre, the Olympic Games, geometry, and thinkers who asked questions. Words such as democracy, theatre and athlete are Greek.
From Rome: roads, arches, concrete and aqueducts. Laws written down for all, a Senate, and Latin words. The names of our months, and the letters we write with: the Latin alphabet.

From India: the digits 0 to 9 and zero as a number. From Persia: a well-run empire of many peoples, and a royal post. From Han China: paper, the wheelbarrow and silk. From the Maya: a zero of their own, and careful calendars.
Historians compare by asking the same questions of each place: who ruled, how people wrote, what they built, believed and traded. A table helps you see what is alike and what is different.

They shared a lot: farming, cities, writing, trade and great buildings. They differed too: Athens let citizens vote, while Han China was run by an emperor and trained officials. Ideas also moved between them along roads and routes.
Some ideas travelled far: Indian digits reached Europe through Arab scholars, and Chinese paper went west along the Silk Road. So the things we use today often come from many peoples, not one.
Try it in the world: make a museum with a room for each civilisation, and put a sign by each thing we still use. Next year: after Rome, the Vikings, Baghdad and the Middle Ages.

exercises.prompt: Match each gift to where it came from.
exercises.hint: Think of Athens, Cai Lun, Brahmagupta and the Romans.
exercises.explain: Democracy: Greece. Paper: Han China. Zero: India. The Latin alphabet: Rome.

exercises.prompt: Which civilisation gave us the Olympic Games?
exercises.hint: They began at Olympia in 776 BC.
exercises.explain: Ancient Greece: the first Olympic Games were held at Olympia, in 776 BC.
Han China, improved by Cai Lun in AD 105.

exercises.prompt: The letters of the English alphabet come from the Romans' Latin alphabet.
exercises.hint: What letters are you reading now?
exercises.explain: True: English is written with the Latin alphabet.

exercises.prompt: Which of these came from the Romans?
exercises.explain: Concrete, arches and aqueducts; the others came from China, India and Greece.

exercises.hint: Athens and Olympia were Greek; Rome's builders and rulers were Roman.
exercises.explain: Greek: democracy, the Olympic Games, Euclid. Roman: aqueducts, the Senate and consuls, Hadrian's Wall.

exercises.hint: The other three come from Latin words for a hundred, a year and water.
exercises.explain: Athlete is Greek; century, annual and aquarium are from Latin.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: All are BC: the biggest number is the earliest.
exercises.explain: 776 BC, 509 BC, about 268 BC, then 27 BC.

exercises.prompt: Which question helps a historian compare civilisations fairly?
exercises.hint: Ask the same kind of question of each one.
exercises.explain: Asking the same questions of each, like who ruled and how, lets you compare fairly.

exercises.prompt: Ideas and inventions moved between civilisations along trade routes.
exercises.hint: Think of Buddhism and paper on the Silk Road.
exercises.explain: True: goods and ideas travelled along roads and routes.

exercises.prompt: The first Olympic Games were in 776 BC and the Colosseum opened in AD 80. How many years apart? Remember: there is no year 0.
exercises.hint: Count the years up to AD 1, then the years after it.
exercises.explain: From 776 BC to AD 1 is 776 years; from AD 1 to AD 80 is 79 more. 776 + 79 = 855 years.

exercises.prompt: What did Athens and Han China do differently?
exercises.hint: Look at the 'ruled by' column of the table.
choices: Athens' citizens voted; China had an emperor
exercises.explain: In Athens citizens voted on laws; Han China was run by an emperor and his officials.

exercises.prompt: Why do we do sums with Indian digits, not Roman numerals?
exercises.hint: Try adding MMXXVI and CDXCIX in your head.
choices: place value and zero make sums easy
Indian digits are older than writing
exercises.explain: With place value and zero, digits line up in columns, so written sums are quick.

exercises.prompt: How were Rome and Persia alike?
exercises.hint: Think of the Royal Road and Roman roads.
choices: both built long roads across their empires
exercises.explain: Both ruled huge empires and built long roads so soldiers and messages could travel fast.

exercises.prompt: The Maya learned their calendars from the Romans.
exercises.hint: Did the Maya and the Romans ever meet?
exercises.explain: False: the Maya, in the Americas, had no contact with Rome and made their own calendars.

exercises.prompt: Why is it hard to call one civilisation 'the best'?
exercises.hint: Think of what each one gave us.
choices: each was good at different things
they all had the same inventions
they all lived in one city
exercises.explain: Each was good at different things and gave us different gifts, so comparing is fairer than ranking.

exercises.prompt: Sort the gifts by where they came from.
exercises.hint: Two civilisations had a zero. Which one used a shell?
exercises.explain: Han China: paper, the wheelbarrow and silk. India: the digits 0 to 9. The Maya: careful calendars and their own zero, drawn as a shell.

exercises.prompt: Follow the journey of the digits 0 to 9, from where they began to you.
items: Arab scholars use and share them.
European traders and scholars learn them.
You use them in maths today.
exercises.hint: The lesson says the digits reached Europe through Arab scholars.
exercises.explain: The digits began in India. Arab scholars used them and passed them on, and Europeans learned them from Arab books. So the digits you write today come from many peoples, not one.
